lessons.title: Raising Equity in the Public Market: IPOs, QIPs, Rights Issues and Preferential Allotments

children.text: A private company raising equity negotiates with one investor at a time. A listed company can go to thousands of investors at once, repeatedly, through routes with fixed rules and timetables. That is the real prize of listing: not the IPO itself, but permanent access to the equity market afterwards.
There are four routes an Indian company uses, and they are not interchangeable. Each has its own regulator-set process, speed and audience.

body.caption: The four public equity routes in India

cells: Institutions, non-institutional investors and retail, in fixed proportions
First listing, raising growth capital and giving early investors an exit
Days once approvals are in place
A listed company raising large sums quickly
Existing shareholders, in proportion to what they hold
Raising money without changing who owns the company
Bringing in a strategic partner, or promoters putting money in

body.text: Listing is not one fundraise. It converts a company into an entity that can raise equity again and again, from a market that is already holding its shares and already pricing them every day.

children.text: Route 1: The IPO
An initial public offer is the first sale of shares to the public, followed by listing on NSE and BSE. Under SEBI's ICDR Regulations the process is tightly scripted.

body.title: How an Indian IPO actually runs

events.title: Preparation
events.description: Appoint merchant bankers, restate financials, clean up the group structure, convert to a public limited company and settle the fresh issue and offer for sale split.

events.title: DRHP filed
events.description: The draft red herring prospectus goes to SEBI and the exchanges, and becomes a public document.

events.title: SEBI observations
events.description: SEBI issues comments. The company responds, updates disclosures and waits for clearance.

events.title: RHP and price band
events.description: The red herring prospectus is filed with the price band, and the roadshow begins.

events.title: Anchor book
events.description: Anchor investors are allotted shares a working day before the issue opens, with a lock-in.

events.title: The issue is open
events.description: Retail applications come in through ASBA and UPI. Money is blocked in the bank account, not debited.

events.title: Listing
events.description: Allotment is finalised, refunds and unblocking happen, and trading begins on the third working day after the issue closes, mandatory for issues opening from 1 December 2023.

children.text: Who gets how much is not left to the company. In a standard book-built issue by a company that meets SEBI's profitability and net worth conditions, the net offer is split in fixed proportions.

body.text: A company that does not meet those eligibility conditions can still list, but under Regulation 6(2) of the ICDR Regulations the split changes sharply: at least 75% to QIBs, up to 15% to non-institutional investors and only up to 10% to retail. Loss-making new-age companies typically list this way. If retail allocation is 10%, that tells you something about the issuer before you read a single financial statement.

body.title: Size the retail bucket
body.prompt: A profitable company launches a ₹1,200 crore book-built IPO under the standard route, with 35% reserved for retail individual investors. How large is the retail portion, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 35% of ₹1,200 crore is ₹420 crore. Under the Regulation 6(2) route the same issue would reserve only 10%, or ₹120 crore, for retail.

body.label: The largest Indian IPO, and the company received none of it
body.context: India's largest IPO at the time was structured entirely as an offer for sale by the Korean parent, Hyundai Motor Company, which sold about 17.5% of the Indian subsidiary. Not a rupee of fresh issue was included, so the listed Indian company received nothing from its own IPO. Always separate the fresh issue from the offer for sale before deciding what an IPO means for the business.

children.text: Route 2: The QIP, the Fastest Door
Once a company has been listed for at least a year, it can raise money from
qualified institutional buyers

through a qualified institutional placement under Chapter VI of the ICDR Regulations. There is no offer document for retail investors and no drawn-out SEBI review, which is why a QIP can close in days.

markDefs.definition: Institutions such as mutual funds, insurers, banks, pension funds and foreign portfolio investors, defined under SEBI regulations. Shortened to QIBs.

children.text: The price is not free. The floor comes from a formula based on recent market prices.

body.latex: \text{Floor price} = \text{Average of the weekly highs and lows of closing prices over the two preceding weeks}
body.caption: A special resolution may permit a discount of up to 5% to this floor

body.title: Price the QIP
body.prompt: A listed company calculates its QIP floor price at ₹500 per share and its shareholders have approved the maximum permitted discount. What is the lowest price at which it can place the shares, in ₹?
body.explanation: 5% of ₹500 is ₹25, so the lowest permitted price is ₹475. The pricing formula exists to stop a listed company issuing shares cheaply to favoured institutions at the expense of existing shareholders.

children.text: Only QIBs can participate, so retail shareholders are diluted without an opportunity to take part.
At least 10% of the issue must go to mutual funds, which prevents the entire placement going to one or two buyers.
The company must have been listed for at least a year, and the issue needs a special resolution.

body.text: Indian banks and NBFCs are heavy users of QIPs, because a bank's capital ratios can require fresh equity at short notice and institutional investors understand the business well. Watch for a flurry of QIPs whenever the market is running high: companies raise equity when their own shares are expensive.

children.text: Route 3: The Rights Issue, the Fair Door

A rights issue offers new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to what they already hold, under Section 62(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013. Nobody is diluted if everybody participates, which makes it the fairest route and a favourite of promoter-heavy Indian companies.
Here is how the arithmetic works. Suppose you hold 400 shares of a company trading at ₹300. It announces a 1:4 rights issue at ₹200 per share, meaning one new share for every four held.

body.caption: A 1:4 rights issue at ₹200, market price ₹300

body.title: Find the ex-rights price
body.prompt: Using the rights issue above, what is the theoretical price per share once the rights shares are issued, in ₹?
body.explanation: Total value is 400 shares at ₹300 plus ₹20,000 paid, which is ₹1,40,000, spread across 500 shares. That gives ₹280. The share price falls from ₹300 to ₹280 not because anything went wrong, but because cheaper shares have been added.

children.text: If you do not want to put in more money, you are not stuck. Your
rights entitlement

is credited to your demat account and can be sold on NSE or BSE during the rights trading window. Someone else buys the right to subscribe, and you receive cash instead of dilution. Doing nothing at all is the only genuinely bad outcome: the entitlement lapses worthless and your stake shrinks.

markDefs.definition: A tradable instrument credited to a shareholder's demat account in a rights issue, representing the right to buy new shares at the offer price. It can be used, sold on the exchange, or allowed to lapse.

body.text: This is the most commonly wasted opportunity in Indian retail investing. Rights entitlements expire. If you get an email about a rights issue and ignore it, you have chosen to be diluted for nothing.

children.text: Route 4: Preferential Allotment, the Targeted Door

A preferential allotment issues shares to specific named investors: a strategic partner, a private equity fund, or very often the promoters themselves putting more money into their own company. It needs a special resolution and follows a pricing formula under Chapter V of the ICDR Regulations.
For a frequently traded share, the price cannot be below the higher of the 90 trading day
volume weighted average price
and the 10 trading day VWAP, calculated to a defined relevant date. Shares allotted are locked in, and the lock-in is longer for promoter allottees than for others.

markDefs.definition: The average traded price over a period, weighted by the quantity traded at each price. Shortened to VWAP, and used in SEBI pricing formulas.

columns.label: Rights issue
points: Offered to every existing shareholder pro rata
No shareholder is diluted if everyone participates
Entitlements can be sold on the exchange
Slower, with a longer document and process
Price is set by the company, often at a meaningful discount

columns.label: Preferential allotment
points: Offered only to named investors
Every other shareholder is diluted, with no choice
Nothing to trade or renounce
Faster and more targeted
Price is floored by a SEBI formula, and allotted shares are locked in

body.title: Pick the route
body.question: A listed midcap NBFC needs ₹2,000 crore within the next three weeks to support loan growth, and is willing to raise it entirely from institutions. Which route fits?
options: A preferential allotment to retail investors
body.explanation: The company is already listed, so an IPO is impossible. A rights issue would take longer and depends on thousands of shareholders acting. A QIP is built precisely for this: large, institutional and fast. Preferential allotment to retail investors is not a route at all.

body.title: Read the signal
body.question: The promoters of a listed company subscribe to a preferential allotment, putting ₹300 crore of their own money into the company at a price set by the SEBI formula, with a lock-in. What does this most likely signal?
options: The promoters are exiting the business
The promoters are raising their stake and committing capital, which is usually read as confidence
Retail shareholders are being given the same opportunity
body.explanation: Promoters putting in fresh money at a formula-driven price, with shares locked in, is generally read as a positive signal. Note what it is not: other shareholders are diluted and are not offered the same chance, which is exactly what a rights issue would have done differently.

body.title: The QIP gate
body.textWithBlank: To use the QIP route, a company's shares of the same class must have been listed for at least ___ year before the notice for the shareholder meeting approving the issue.
body.explanation: The one-year listing condition ensures there is enough market price history for the floor price formula to mean anything.

body.title: What about SME IPOs on NSE Emerge and BSE SME?

children.text: Smaller companies can list on the dedicated SME platforms, NSE Emerge and the BSE SME platform, with lighter eligibility requirements and smaller issue sizes than the main board. Lot sizes are larger, so retail participation needs a bigger cheque, and liquidity after listing is usually thin.

After a surge in SME listings and several instances of aggressive pricing, SEBI tightened these norms in late 2024, adding conditions including an operating profit requirement before listing and limits on how much of the issue can be an offer for sale. The rules in this segment have changed more than once, so check the current NSE or BSE eligibility criteria rather than relying on a summary.

For a founder, the honest question is whether the company is ready for quarterly disclosure and public scrutiny at all. Listing is a permanent change in how a business operates, not a one-off fundraise.
What Listing Costs You

body.title: The trade a company makes when it lists

columns.label: What the company gains
points: Access to a very large pool of capital
Repeat access through QIPs, rights issues and FPOs
A market price, useful as acquisition currency and for ESOPs
An exit route for early investors and employees
Credibility with customers, lenders and talent

columns.label: What the company gives up
points: Quarterly results and continuous disclosure under SEBI LODR
Insider trading rules binding on promoters and employees
A share price that reacts to every piece of news
Significant issue costs and ongoing compliance cost
Pressure to manage for the next quarter, not the next decade

body.title: Three ways to raise ₹600 crore
body.scenario: You are in the finance team of a listed Indian specialty chemicals company with a ₹6,000 crore market capitalisation. The board wants to raise ₹600 crore for a new plant. The promoter family holds 52% and does not want to fall below 50%. A large global chemicals group has separately expressed interest in taking a strategic stake. The CFO asks you to lay out the options.
body.prompt: Compare a QIP, a rights issue and a preferential allotment for this specific company, and say which you would recommend.
body.modelAnswer:
QIP: fastest and cleanest execution, priced off the two-week formula with up to 5% discount. It raises ₹600 crore from institutions in days. The catch is the promoter stake: issuing roughly 10% new equity takes the family from 52% to about 47%, which breaches their stated constraint. They cannot participate in a QIP themselves.

Rights issue: the promoter family can protect its 52% by subscribing to its full entitlement, which means finding about ₹312 crore of family money. If they can, this is the fairest route and every shareholder gets the same opportunity. If they cannot, they can renounce part of their entitlement and still slip below 50%, so the decision rests entirely on the family's own liquidity. It is also slower, and if the market falls during the process, subscription can disappoint.

Preferential allotment to the strategic investor: brings ₹600 crore plus a partner with industry capability, priced off the 90-day and 10-day VWAP formula with a lock-in. The promoter family still falls below 50%, and now a large industry player sits on the register with whatever rights are negotiated. Worth noting that crossing certain thresholds can also trigger takeover code obligations, which needs legal input early.

Recommendation: start by testing the family's appetite and ability to fund a rights issue, because it is the only route that satisfies the stated 50% constraint. If they cannot, then the real conversation is not about instruments at all, it is whether holding above 50% is worth more to them than the plant. Falling to 47% with a strong institutional register is not a loss of control in practice, given board composition and the fact that no other single holder is anywhere near them.

body.title: Reading any Indian equity issue announcement
steps: Which route is it: IPO, FPO, QIP, rights issue or preferential allotment?
How much is fresh issue and how much is offer for sale?
What will the money be used for, as stated in the objects of the issue?
At what price, and how does that compare to the current market price?
Who is allowed to participate, and are existing retail shareholders included?
How much dilution results, and what happens to the promoter holding?
If it is a rights issue you are eligible for, what is the last date to subscribe or sell the entitlement?

body.label: SEBI: Public Issues Filings
body.description: Draft and final offer documents for Indian public issues. Open any DRHP and read the "Objects of the Issue" and "Capital Structure" sections to see the fresh issue and offer for sale split for yourself.

cards.definition: First sale of shares to the public, followed by listing on NSE and BSE.
Draft red herring prospectus, the offer document filed with SEBI before an IPO.
Institutions allotted shares a working day before the issue opens, with a lock-in.
Qualified institutional placement. Fast issue to QIBs by a company listed for at least a year.
Average of weekly highs and lows of closing prices over the two preceding weeks, with up to 5% discount permitted.
Pro-rata offer of new shares to existing shareholders under Section 62(1)(a).
A tradable right to subscribe to a rights issue, credited to your demat account.
Issue to named investors, priced off the 90 and 10 trading day VWAP formula, with a lock-in.

points: Listing matters less for the IPO itself than for the repeat access it creates to QIPs, rights issues and preferential allotments.
In a standard book-built IPO the split is up to 50% QIB, at least 15% non-institutional and at least 35% retail. Under Regulation 6(2) it becomes 75, 15 and 10.
An IPO that is entirely an offer for sale brings the company no money at all, as Hyundai Motor India showed in 2024.
A QIP is the fastest route for a listed company, but only institutions can participate and the price is floored by formula.
A rights issue dilutes nobody who participates, and entitlements can be sold on the exchange if you do not want to subscribe.
A preferential allotment is fast and targeted, dilutes everyone else, and comes with SEBI pricing rules and lock-ins.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Regulatory thresholds described are summaries of SEBI and Companies Act provisions as they stood when written, and these change. Verify current requirements in the relevant regulations or with a merchant banker or company secretary before acting. Nothing here is a recommendation to apply for any issue.
